item.title: Almost Optimal Lower Bounds under Almost ETH for Approximating Euclidean k-means
item.description: arXiv:2611.14892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the Euclidean $k$-means problem, we are given a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and the goal is to find $k$ representative points in space so as to minimize the sum of the squared distances from each point to its closest representative. Algorithmically, de la Vega, Karpinski, Kenyon, and Rabani [STOC'03] and Kumar, Sabharwal, and Sen [JACM'10] obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for high-dimensional Euclidean $k$-means in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{O(1)}} \cdot dn^{O(1)}$, which was subsequently improved to $2^{\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon)} + O(ndk)$ by Feldman, Monemizadeh, and Sohler [SoCG'07]. On the lower-bound side, a recent work of Cohen-Addad, Karthik, Saulpic, and Schwiegelshohn [SoCG'26] proposed the Exponential Time for Expanders Hypothesis (XXH), which asserts exponential-time hardness for $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximating Vertex Cover on vertex expanders, and used it to prove nearly matching running time lower bound whenever $k=\tilde{\omega}(1/\varepsilon)$. We observe that XXH does not hold in the parameter regime needed for the above result, and show how to repair their reduction under a more standard assumption. More precisely, we show that assuming the Almost Exponential Time Hypothesis for 3-SAT (Almost ETH), for every constant $\beta\in(0,1)$, Euclidean $k$-means in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has no $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{1-\beta}}\text{poly}(n,d)$, whenever $k=\tilde{\omega}(1/\varepsilon)$. By modifying the construction, we also obtain a similar result for approximating the Euclidean $k$-median problem.
item.dc:creator: Karthik C. S., Dor Minzer

item.title: A Linear-Time Construction on $\mathbb{S}^2$ Achieving a Sublinear Energy Gap on Smale's Seventh Problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.15783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smale's seventh problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm that places $N$ points on the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^2$ with logarithmic energy (the sum of $-\log$ of all pairwise distances) within $O(\log N)$ of the minimum. The minimal energy has an asymptotic expansion with explicit terms of order $N^2$ and $N\log N$ and a linear term whose constant is unknown. Brauchart, Hardin, and Saff conjectured this constant; the resulting expansion, $E_{BHS}(N)$, is known to be an upper bound on the minimum, up to $o(N)$. All previously analyzed constructions on $\mathbb{S}^2$ have energy exceeding $E_{BHS}(N)$ by an amount that grows at least linearly in $N$, i.e. $\Omega(N)$, far from the $O(\log N)$ accuracy sought by Smale. We present TerracedZonal, a deterministic construction that generates $N$ points in $\Theta(N)$ time and memory. Points are placed on latitude rings whose populations are held constant across bands ("terraces") chosen by a one-dimensional dynamic program, so that adjacent rings within each terrace lock into a staggered triangular lattice. Under a locality assumption, we prove that the energy exceeds $E_{BHS}(N)$ by only $\Theta(N^{2/3})$, with an explicit constant; exact evaluation up to $N = 10^9$ confirms this rate. Under the same assumption, its distance from the true minimum is sublinear if the conjecture holds. To our knowledge, this is the first algorithmic construction with a sublinear excess over $E_{BHS}(N)$ of explicit order (proven under the locality assumption), a necessary step toward Smale's seventh problem. With one parameter changed, the same algorithm also gives an equal-weight integration rule on $\mathbb{S}^2$ that runs just as fast and whose error decays at an empirical rate of $N^{-4}$ on smooth functions, versus $N^{-3/2}$ for every previous fast construction we tested.
item.dc:creator: Rishabh Kabra, Wim Dehaen, Andrea Karlova, Mark Hamilton, Joao Carreira, Maks Ovsjanikov, Jonathan T. Barron

item.title: Delaunay-Based Nearest Neighbor Search with Grid-Accelerated Queries and Parallel Construction
item.description: arXiv:2611.15320v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nearest-neighbor search is a fundamental primitive in computer graphics, with applications in distance field computation, surface reconstruction, and point cloud registration. In many graphics applications, data points lie on a surface manifold embedded in 3D space, whereas queries are distributed throughout the surrounding volume, a setting in which spatial partitioning structures such as k-d trees and grids can become inefficient. Dynamic-programming-based nearest-neighbor search (DP-NNS) offers an alternative: it traverses a successor DAG that records the history of incremental Delaunay construction and often outperforms spatial partitioning structures. However, its sequential construction is slow, and naive parallelization degrades query performance, limiting its practical adoption. We accelerate both queries and construction in DP-NNS. For queries, we introduce a grid-based initialization strategy that precomputes valid starting points on the successor DAG, shortening search paths while preserving exactness and enabling a twofold speedup. For construction, we analyze how parallel insertion affects query cost and develop a parallel algorithm that preserves logarithmic expected query cost under stated geometric assumptions. Our parallel construction algorithm achieves a 10x speedup over the sequential baseline while maintaining nearly the same query cost. We further reorder query points to improve cache locality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms widely used libraries in nearest-neighbor query performance.
item.dc:creator: Pengfei Wang, Shiqing Xin, Changhe Tu

item.title: Bounded Knapsack in Truly Subquadratic Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.15792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bounded Knapsack asks how many copies of each item to take to maximize profit under a capacity constraint. Given $n$ records with binary-encoded multiplicities, we return optimal counts in randomized time with a fixed power saving in the maximum item weight $w_{\max}$ or maximum item profit $p_{\max}$. Fix $1<\rho<2$ and suppose integer $(\min,+)$-convolution on length-$m$ arrays can be computed with failure probability at most $\eta$ in $\widetilde O(m^\rho)$ time, up to polynomial factors in the entry bit length and $\log(1/\eta)$. Put $f(\rho)=4(3-\rho)/(8-3\rho).$ For any fixed $\epsilon>0$, on inputs whose integers have magnitude polynomial in $n+\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})$, our algorithm runs in time $$\widetilde O\bigl(n\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})^{f(\rho)+\epsilon}\bigr).$$ It returns optimal counts with high probability. If convolution saves $\delta=2-\rho$ in its exponent, knapsack retains $\delta/(1+3\delta/2)$. With the integer convolution exponent $1.9601397040925$, a separate parameter choice gives $\widetilde O(n+\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})^{1.961})$, including for 0-1 Knapsack. We keep the copies compressed. Witnessed convolutions generate residual queries, and local linear programs filter them by cost. Resilient lattice cores allow recursive states to coalesce. Progression reserves support rounding, and a thin affordable fiber yields a lift that reduces the normalized column volume. This volume bounds the number of LP regions a grid lookup examines.
item.dc:creator: Huanyi Zhou

item.title: Visibility graphs of irregularly sampled two-dimensional fields via Voronoi tessellations
item.description: arXiv:2611.16336v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visibility graphs map a time series into a network by linking two data whenever the straight line between them is not obstructed by intermediate data. Their extension to two-dimensional fields has so far been restricted to regular lattices, where visibility is checked along a finite number of lattice directions. We propose a definition for scalar data sampled at arbitrary, irregularly scattered points of the plane. Each point is assigned its Voronoi cell, so that the data become a landscape of prisms, and two points are linked when the line of sight between them clears the cells crossed by the connecting segment. This yields horizontal ($\HVGV$) and natural ($\NVGV$) Voronoi visibility graphs that reduce exactly to the classical horizontal and natural visibility graphs when the points are collinear, contain the Gabriel graph of the point set, and can be built by an exact walk through the Delaunay triangulation. For uncorrelated heights, the horizontal graph depends only on the ranks of the data, so its statistics are independent of the marginal distribution. The probability that two points see each other is $2/[(M+1)(M+2)]$, where $M$ is the number of Voronoi cells crossed, which reduces the problem to the geometry of the tessellation. For Poisson points this gives a degree distribution with a scale-free tail $P(k)\simeq(\pi^3/4)\,k^{-2}$ and a mean degree that grows as $(\pi^3/8)\ln N$, in contrast with the finite value $\langle k\rangle=4$ of one-dimensional series. Two dimensions are therefore the marginal case in which isotropic horizontal visibility ceases to be local. Numerical simulations with up to $N=1.28\times10^5$ points support these predictions.
item.dc:creator: Francisco J. Mu\~noz, Juan Carlos Nu\~no

item.title: An upper bound on the number of edges of a Gomory corner polyhedron
item.description: arXiv:2611.16839v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish the first nontrivial upper bound on the number of edges of a Gomory corner polyhedron, resolving a long-standing open question. For an $n$-dimensional corner polyhedron associated with an integer lattice of determinant $\delta$, the number of edges is at most $$ O\left(n6^n \cdot \bigl(1+\log_2(2\delta)\bigr)^{2n-3}\right). $$ This improves the standard bound obtained by counting pairs of vertices, reducing the logarithmic exponent from $(2n-2)$ to $(2n-3)$.
item.dc:creator: A. Yu. Chirkov, S. I. Veselov, D. V. Gribanov, D. S. Malyshev, N. Yu. Zolotykh

item.title: Optimal Polyomino Fences
item.description: arXiv:2611.16883v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The $n$-omino fence problem asks how many cells can be surrounded by placing every $n$-omino exactly once in the grid. We present a new dynamic programming approach for this problem, allowing us to prove optimality for the pentomino and hexomino fence and to classify all possible pentomino orders by optimal area. For the first time we also provide strong heuristic solutions and upper bounds for all fences up to $n = 15$, after which we even approximate the $500$-omino fence with computational experiments. Finally, we generalize the problem to 3D, where we prove optimality for pentacubes and derive heuristic solutions for hexacubes and heptacubes.
item.dc:creator: Alexis Langlois-R\'emillard, Mia N. M\"u{\ss}ig, Helmut Podhaisky, Erika Roldan, G\"unter Rote, Maximilian Br\"omme, Matthes Norden, Maximilian Prietzel, Daniel Yu, Mykhailo Lyader

item.title: Asymptotic Dimension of Persistence Modules of Bounded Presentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.16965v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We compute the asymptotic dimension of spaces of multiparameter persistence modules of bounded presentation under the interleaving distance. The $d$-parameter modules with at most $n$ generators and $m$ relations have asymptotic dimension, and Assouad-Nagata dimension, exactly $d(n+m)$, the number of coordinates of their generator and relation grades, over every field; for two parameters this is $2(n+m)$. The space has continuous moduli, already for two parameters and $n,m\ge2$: over an infinite field it contains, at every scale, infinite uniformly separated families of pairwise non-isomorphic modules with one fibered barcode, so it is not doubling even at a fixed fibered barcode; already for $m\ge1$ it is not coarsely equivalent to a proper metric space. The proof is an induction on the number of distinct grade coordinates: an interleaving small compared with the gaps between these coordinates moves each of them by at most twice its size and preserves the induced grid representation, so the continuous moduli are invisible at large scale. Each class of modules at finite distance therefore embeds coarsely into Hilbert space; for $n,m\ge2$ over an uncountable field, the classes that contain these families admit no such embedding into a separable Hilbert space. Under the two-parameter matching distance $2(n+m)$ is a lower bound, attained for one generator and for two generators with at most one relation; on a finite net of $S$ slices the asymptotic dimension is at most $2nS$.
item.dc:creator: Sushovan Majhi, Atish Mitra, \v{Z}iga Virk

item.title: Sheaf-Inspired Structured Scoring Extensions of LightGCN for Collaborative Filtering
item.description: arXiv:2611.17226v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Graph-based collaborative filtering learns user and item representations by propagating embeddings over a user--item interaction graph. We investigate a modular, sheaf-inspired scoring extension placed on top of a three-layer LightGCN backbone. The motivation comes from cellular sheaves, where local vector spaces are related by linear restriction maps; here, this idea motivates structured, pair-dependent transformations of user and item embeddings rather than a change to graph propagation. We compare the identity inner-product scorer, diagonal, rank-one low-rank, and full matrix residual scorers, and a parameter-matched residual MLP baseline (\texttt{mlp\_full}) on Amazon-Book, Gowalla, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp2018. We report ranking quality and catalog coverage at cutoffs 10 and 20. The selected structured variants show modest, dataset-dependent changes in ranking quality and sometimes substantial changes in coverage. Our method is inspired by sheaf geometry but does not construct a cellular sheaf or implement sheaf-Laplacian diffusion; the experiments therefore do not establish a causal benefit from sheaf geometry itself.
item.dc:creator: Ksenia Belkovskaya, Timur Lidzhiev, Maria Stebliy, Alexander Tarakanov

item.title: Finite Automata Encoding Piecewise Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2104.02876v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Finite automata are used to encode geometric figures and functions. The original approach is to represent each point of a figure in $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a convolution of its $n$ coordinates written in some base. Then a figure is said to be encoded as a finite automaton if the set of convolutions corresponding to the points in this figure is accepted by a B\"{u}chi automaton. The only differentiable functions which can be encoded as a finite automaton in this way are linear. This paper proposes a discretization of the original approach in which we change points as building blocks of a function to hierarchical tensor product B-splines. This reduces an uncountable set of points representing a function to a countable set of splines that enables us to use finite automata instead of B\"uchi automata. Moreover, it allows to represent a rich family of piecewise polynomial functions with arbitrary degrees of smoothness that can approximate any continuous functions defined on a compact domain arbitrarily close. We consider such piecewise polynomial functions with unbounded support and demonstrate that finite automata allow to handle computational tasks arising in the framework of hierarchical splines in polynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Dmitry Berdinsky, Prohrak Kruengthomya

item.title: 2-Layer Fan-Planarity in Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2508.17349v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding whether a bipartite graph admits a 2-layer fan-planar drawing. This resolves an open problem posed in several papers since 2015. We also obtain a linear-time algorithm for the one-sided case.
item.dc:creator: Yasuaki Kobayashi, Yuto Okada

item.title: Minimum central circles: chain order, seam obstructions, and exact finite certification
item.description: arXiv:2607.28654v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We minimize the radius of a central circle externally tangent to pairwise non-overlapping circles of radii $1,2,\ldots,n$. We first study the adjacent-chain relaxation, which imposes only the constraints between consecutive circles. Its angular kernel has strict anti-Monge structure, so Supnick's classical theorem supplies a fixed minimizing cyclic order at every central radius. A monotonicity argument transfers this order to the chain-radius problem. Full geometric feasibility requires every pairwise angular constraint. We give a self-contained criterion for feasibility of the canonical Supnick necklace on $\{k,\ldots,n\}$ at its chain root, expressed by one seam deficit. For every fixed $k$ the seam eventually fails and its failure persists. We prove the complete classifications for $k=1,2,3$, whose first failures occur at $n=8,13,17$, respectively. For the global infimum, we certify rational brackets $L_n<R^*(n)\le U_n$ of exact width $10^{-11}$ for every $3\le n\le14$. The lower proof combines independently enclosed angles, integer dynamic programming, and complete cyclic-order coverage; the upper proof uses exact rational Cartesian witnesses. The certificate does not depend on floating-point pruning in the numerical search. We distinguish these finite brackets and fixed-order theorems from numerical descriptions of floating circles and from unresolved claims about all optimal placements.
item.dc:creator: Maurizio Falconi

item.title: Computing Projective Implicit Representations from Poset Towers
item.description: arXiv:2505.08755v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A family of simplicial complexes connected by simplicial maps and indexed by a finite poset $P$ is called a poset tower. Poset towers subsume multi-parameter filtrations, zigzag filtrations, and one-parameter simplicial towers, while allowing arbitrary finite posets and simplicial maps. The homology of a poset tower is a $P$-persistence module. To compute it globally over $P$, we consider the chain complex segment of $P$-persistence modules $C_{\ell-1}\xleftarrow{\partial_{\ell}}C_\ell \xleftarrow{\partial_{\ell+1}}C_{\ell+1}$ induced by the simplices of the tower. Unlike in one-critical multi-filtrations, the chain modules $C_\ell$ need not be projective and may have a complicated structure. We address the problem of replacing this segment by projective modules and $P$-graded matrices while preserving homology. The resulting projective implicit representation (PiRep) plays the role of the graded boundary-matrix representation in the classical persistence algorithm: it converts simplicial data into algebraic input on which persistent homology can be computed globally over $P$. In particular, a PiRep can be used as input to algorithms for computing minimal presentations of persistent homology. We give an efficient algorithm to compute a PiRep from a poset tower. It constructs degreewise minimal presentations and asymptotically minimal second terms of projective resolutions of the chain modules $C_\ell$, lifts the boundary maps $\partial_\ell$ to these resolutions, and assembles the resulting data into a PiRep using an additional correction term. The method is tailored to chain complexes induced by poset towers and computes the required algebraic data combinatorially, exploiting their special structure and avoiding general-purpose algebraic reduction. In the context of poset towers, it is fully general and can serve as a foundation for efficient algorithms on specific posets.
item.dc:creator: Tamal K. Dey, Florian Russold

item.title: Minimum central circles: an effective characterization of the global asymptotic constant
item.description: arXiv:2609.13630v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $R^\ast(n)$ be the minimum radius of a central circle externally tangent to nonoverlapping circles of radii $1,\ldots,n$. We prove that $R^\ast(n)=C_\ast n^2+o(n^2)$ and give finite linear programs that enclose $C_\ast$ with prescribed error. An exact angular comparison reduces the problem to marked points on a line with separation at least the geometric mean of each pair of marks. Concatenation with bounded joining cost and reassignment to the prescribed normalized radii prove existence of the limit. Balanced finite-word programs give a bracket of width $(1/k+1/r)/\pi$, before directed arithmetic error, using $k$ types and words of length $r$. We also obtain explicit geometric bounds. For the upper bound, we recover finite and countable reflected-block constructions by actual permutations, retaining all pair constraints. A coupled terminal-subset argument gives an explicit lower bound strictly above $1/8$. Together these give $C_{\rm term}+\eta_{\rm width}\le C_\ast\le U_4$. The lower endpoint comes from the terminal-subset argument, and the upper endpoint from the four-block construction; neither is asserted sharp. The finite-word scheme establishes computability; efficient high-precision evaluation and the structure of global optimizers remain open.
item.dc:creator: Maurizio Falconi

item.title: A linear edge bound for k-quasi-planar graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.01509v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove the $k$-quasi-planar graph conjecture for topological drawings. For every integer $k\ge 2$, a simple graph on $n\ge 3$ vertices admitting a drawing with no $k$ pairwise crossing edges has at most $1056(k-1)^2(n-2)$ edges. Thus the number of edges is linear in $n$, with an explicit quadratic dependence on $k$. The result allows multiple crossings between the same pair of edges, including edges with a common endpoint. The proof uses the double of a sphere with boundary to represent graph edges by closed geodesics on a hyperbolic surface. The endpoints of geodesic lifts induce partial orders of width at most $k-1$. A stability bound for greedy chain partitions, together with a counting argument over a triangulation, gives the stated edge bound.
item.dc:creator: Ankan Sadhu

item.title: Resolving Tusn\'ady's Problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.06998v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove a lower bound of $\Omega_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ for the worst-case combinatorial discrepancy of $N$-point sets with respect to anchored boxes in every fixed dimension $d\ge3$. Together with Nikolov's upper bound of the same order and Wei's planar lower bound, this settles Tusn\'ady's problem: the discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes is $\Theta_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. The proof combines smoothed product test functions, sampling discretization, and an entropy argument for conditioned Gaussian vectors. The matching upper and lower bounds are also formalized in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Wengiel
